procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 08.12.2010 in CWP No. 19909 of 2010, specifically the second part of the order directing the Senior Superintendent of Police, Ludhiana to register a criminal case against Rishi Pal Singh and submit an Action Taken Report.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court disposed of CWP No. 19909/2010 with two directions: 1) The petition was rendered infructuous because the shop (premises) of STC were de-sealed during the pendency of the petition. 2) A criminal case should be registered against Rishi Pal Singh, an officer of the State, for filing a false affidavit, and an Action Taken Report should be submitted to the Court within three months.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Punjab appealed the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal of the State and disposed of the connected appeal.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal of the State is allowed and the connected appeal is disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in passing directions for registering a criminal investigation against the Assistant Excise and Taxation Commissioner, holding that he had filed an affidavit taking a false defence in a writ petition concerning the illegal sealing of a shop.

facts: A company filed a writ petition in the High Court, alleging that officers from the Department of Excise and Taxation had illegally sealed its shop.
The Assistant Excise and Taxation Commissioner (AETC) filed an affidavit in response, denying that the shop had been sealed.

The High Court, upon reviewing the case, concluded that the AETC's affidavit was false. It based this conclusion on a photograph showing the sealed shop and its suspicion that an official order and a corresponding entry in the dispatch register had been antedated and forged.

As a result, while disposing of the writ petition (which had become infructuous because the shop was de-sealed), the High Court directed the police to register a criminal case (FIR) against the AETC for filing a false defence.
law: Courts should not pass adverse remarks against a person unless it is absolutely necessary for the proper adjudication of the case.

Principles of natural justice require that a person must be given an opportunity to be heard (show cause) before adverse findings or directions are made against them, especially if they are not a party to the dispute.
Judicial remarks should be governed by principles of justice, fair play, and restraint, reflecting sobriety and moderation.
Passing such orders against government officers without proper justification can have a demoralizing effect on honest officials.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had acted against the principles of natural justice by ordering a criminal investigation without making the AETC a party to the case or giving him an opportunity to explain the circumstances.
The Court re-examined the evidence and found the High Court's appreciation of the facts to be "incorrect and erroneous."

Specifically, the Supreme Court reviewed the dispatch register and found no evidence of tampering, cutting, or overwriting. It noted that the register contained multiple entries in different languages and scripts, which explained the single English entry that the High Court found suspicious.
The Court also reasoned that the officer had no motive to antedate the communication, as the date in question was already past a deadline previously set by the High Court.
Furthermore, the record showed no evidence that the officer held any personal animus against the company.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's directions were misplaced and would have a demoralizing effect on well-meaning officers working to prevent tax evasion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that it was not justified in ordering a criminal investigation against the officer. The directions were found to be based on an incorrect appreciation of the facts and were passed in violation of the principles of natural justice. Consequently, the Supreme Court expunged the adverse remarks and quashed the criminal proceedings initiated against the officer.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in passing directions for registering a criminal investigation against the Assistant Excise and Taxation Commissioner, holding that he had filed an affidavit taking a false defence in a writ petition concerning the illegal sealing of a shop.
appellant_arguments: The directions were passed without affording the concerned officer an opportunity to explain the facts and circumstances.
The High Court's directions relied only on the assertions made by the respondent, without any evidence to substantiate them.
The language of the entry in the despatch register (English) corresponded to the language of the original document being dispatched, which was also in English.
Passing such an order against an officer who has launched a campaign against tax evaders has a demoralizing effect on honest officers.
respondent_arguments: The respondent did not oppose the appeal in relation to the High Court's observations and directions for a criminal investigation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a court passes remarks against a person whose conduct is under scrutiny, it must satisfy three conditions: (1) the party in question must be before the court or have an opportunity to explain or defend themselves; (2) there must be evidence on record that justifies the remarks; and (3) it must be necessary for the decision of the case to animadvert on that conduct.
obiter: The registration of a criminal investigation against an officer, contrary to settled principles of law, has a demoralizing effect on well-meaning officers of the State.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's conclusions, which led to the direction for a criminal investigation, were based on mere surmises and bald assertions without any material evidence. A review of the record, particularly the despatch register, did not support the High Court's prima facie view that there was any ante-dating or interpolation.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that an adverse order, especially one directing a criminal investigation, cannot be passed against a person without making them a party to the dispute or affording them an opportunity to show cause.
why_respondent_won: The High Court's conclusions were based on mere surmises and/or bald assertions, without any material attesting to the conclusions or regard for consequences.
The record does not support the prime facie view taken by the court below, in regard to ante-dating or interpolation of the despatch register.
Neither was the officer made party to the dispute, nor was he given an opportunity to show cause... before such adverse directions were passed against him.
The respondent (the original writ petitioner) did not oppose the appeal in relation to the observations and directions that were the subject matter of the appeal.
policy_considerations: The impugned directions issued by the High Court... [have] a demoralizing effect on the well-meaning officers of the State.
The directions were totally misplaced, more so, when the endeavour of the officer was to bring the offenders to book and save evasion of duty, mandatorily required to be paid by the assessee.
